doc.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Race in today's jazz scene
summary: He discusses cliques, few black musicians in traditional jazz, Wynton Marsalis, and the Dixieland label.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You can program the CD. What’s your take on the racial atmosphere in today’s jazz scene? Is there one that is prevalent, or not?

Well yeah, it’s kind of a strange subject because I think there’s a lot of sort of cliques and I don’t think it’s always necessarily that the guys don’t want to play together as far as blacks and whites, but I think for some reason it ends up being sort of little like a scene of guys or a clique of guys who are together and then there’s this other clique playing © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

together. And I’m surprised sometimes at how often I’ll play in bands that are all white. And the guys are all open minded people who are not prejudiced, and I think it’s a funny thing. I don’t really understand it. I feel very fortunate that I grew up in a family that was really not prejudiced and put those feelings into me as a kid, and brought me up to feel that way. I think it’s kind of weird. Of course there are prejudiced people out there, musicians and not musicians, and it’s always seemed funny to me how few black people you see at these jazz parties, on the stage and off the stage. Because especially when it’s more toward Dixieland or traditional jazz or whatever you want to call it. I think it just sort of became not the cool thing to do among black people. I don’t really understand it exactly.

There seems to be very few black musicians playing this well — especially Dixieland. Probably down in New Orleans and so forth, but when you go to some of the festivals that have a lot of the Dixieland bands, it’s turned more into, well it’s changed. They have the costumes and all that.

Yeah I don’t know how to answer that question and I think there’s been racial issues regarding Wynton Marsalis and his groups of guys, and I think — I don’t know if he’s been misquoted or not but there was times when people got the impression that he was maybe prejudiced, but I don’t think he necessarily is. I think since these things have become hot topics, I think he’s made a point of having more white people in his bands and stuff like that, and this is just my take on it, I don’t know. It’s kind of an icky subject.
It is. It doesn’t have a good answer, and it could be an answer we don’t want to hear too.

Yeah, exactly. And I think maybe the term “Dixieland” probably turned a lot of black people off. The idea of Dixie and the south and the bad connotations of way down home in Dixie and all that, I don’t know, maybe that’s part of it.
